summary: Utah classifies birds and mammals species-by-species, and the roof rat falls through a gap created by a 2023 rule rewrite. The Division of Wildlife Resources' Bird and Mammal Classification Table 3b-1 (May 1, 2023, incorporated by Utah Admin. Code R657-3b) lists the Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus — the common pet 'fancy rat') as a domestic animal 'not covered under this rule,' but Rattus rattus appears nowhere on it. The table's default makes every unlisted species 'presumed prohibited' and requires a DWR assessment before collection, importation, or possession is authorized. Critically, this is NOT an absolute ban: a lawful pathway exists — a Certificate of Registration (COR) obtained through a case-by-case variance (R657-3a-9) or a species reclassification petition (R657-3a-8) — so keeping, breeding, selling, or importing a captive-bred roof rat is restricted rather than flatly prohibited. Before 2023, the old rule R657-3(32) jointly exempted 'Rats, Norway and Black (Rattus norvegicus and Rattus rattus)' as non-COR pets; the May 2023 simplification kept only the Norway rat, making this a textbook agency-fixable species/enumeration trap.

kit.problem: Utah classifies birds and mammals species-by-species, and the domesticated roof rat (Rattus rattus) falls through a gap. The Division of Wildlife Resources' Bird and Mammal Classification Table 3b-1 (under Admin. Rule R657-3b) names the Norway rat — Rattus norvegicus, the species behind the common pet 'fancy rat' — as a domestic animal 'not covered' by the rule, fully exempt. But Rattus rattus appears nowhere on that table. Under the rule, any unlisted species is 'presumed prohibited' and requires a DWR assessment/authorization before it can be possessed, bred, sold, or imported. So a captive-bred, tame roof rat is not flatly illegal — a lawful pathway exists (a Certificate of Registration obtained through a variance or species reclassification) — but it cannot be legally kept without a prior DWR determination. This is an enumeration gap, not a considered decision that roof rats are dangerous: the near-identical fancy rat is exempt by name, while the roof rat is simply missing. Most tellingly, this gap is brand new. Until the May 1, 2023 rule rewrite, the old rule R657-3(32) explicitly and JOINTLY listed 'Rats, Norway and Black (Rattus norvegicus and Rattus rattus)' as exempt domestic pets — for over a decade captive-bred roof rats had the exact same unregulated status as fancy rats. The 2023 simplification carried only the Norway rat onto the new Table 3b-1 and dropped the roof rat, with no record of any finding that domesticated roof rats are dangerous.
kit.ask: Restore captive-bred, domestic-lineage Rattus rattus to Table 3b-1 as a noncontrolled/domestic-exempt species, alongside the Norway rat that is already listed (and that the roof rat used to share a line with under the pre-2023 rule). Concretely: (1) ask DWR in writing whether the post-2023 omission of R. rattus from Table 3b-1 was intentional, and whether captive-bred R. rattus can be grouped with R. norvegicus as a domestic commensal-rodent strain rather than treated as an unlisted species needing individual assessment; and (2) file (or support) a Request for Species Reclassification under R657-3a-8 ($200 fee) to amend Table 3b-1 to list captive-bred R. rattus as noncontrolled/domestic-exempt, restoring its pre-2023 status. Because the classification lives in an administrative RULE that DWR controls — not a statute — DWR (through the Wildlife Board's rulemaking process) is exactly the body that can fix it.
kit.branch_note: This is the AGENCY/RULE branch, fixable through the Division of Wildlife Resources — not the legislature. The restriction comes from an administrative classification choice, not a statute that bans roof rats. The Utah Code (Title 23A, Wildlife Resources Code) delegates species-classification authority to the DWR and Wildlife Board; the actual list lives in Admin. Rule R657-3b and its incorporated Bird and Mammal Classification Table 3b-1 (May 1, 2023), both of which the DWR drafts and the Wildlife Board adopts. Nothing in statute names or prohibits the roof rat — it is merely absent from a table, which triggers the rule's default 'unlisted = presumed prohibited.' The Norway rat (the fancy rat's species) IS named as domestic-exempt on the same table, and the SAME table jointly listed both rats until the May 2023 rewrite, proving the table is the right instrument and the omission is an enumeration gap, not a policy judgment that roof rats are uniquely dangerous. The fix is therefore an AGENCY action: a written classification clarification/determination from the DWR Certificate of Registration office, and/or a Request for Species Reclassification under R657-3a-8 (Utah Code 63G-3-601 separately lets any person petition an agency to amend a rule) to add captive-bred R. rattus back to Table 3b-1. Two caveats stated plainly: (a) the legislature is NOT the primary lever, because the classification is administrative code, not statutory text — petitioning lawmakers would just redirect you to DWR; and (b) the DR notes the roof rat is entrenched in Utah's own pest manuals as an invasive structural pest, so the reclassification panel (DWR + Dept. of Agriculture & Food + Dept. of Health & Human Services) will demand a strong biosecurity/domestic-lineage case — the realistic near-term win may be a personal-use variance (R657-3a-9) rather than statewide reclassification. Start with the agency: it can both interpret the gap and rewrite the table.

targets.name: Utah Division of Wildlife Resources — Wildlife Registration / Certificate of Registration (COR) office
targets.why: The COR office administers Rule R657-3b and Table 3b-1 — the exact instrument that lists the Norway rat as domestic-exempt and omits the roof rat — and processes both variance requests (R657-3a-9) and species reclassification petitions (R657-3a-8). Ask in writing whether the post-2023 omission of R. rattus was intentional and whether captive-bred R. rattus can be grouped with R. norvegicus or restored to the noncontrolled list. Verified contact (DR): dwrregistration@utah.gov; phone 801-538-4701 / 385-332-6154; mail to 1594 W. North Temple, Suite 2110, Box 146301, Salt Lake City, UT 84114-6301.

targets.name: Utah DWR — Request for Species Reclassification (Utah Admin. Code R657-3a-8)
targets.why: The formal channel to restore captive-bred R. rattus to Table 3b-1's noncontrolled/domestic-exempt list — the same list it shared with R. norvegicus before May 2023. A reclassification petition ($200 fee) compels an interagency review (DWR + Dept. of Agriculture & Food + Dept. of Health & Human Services) and a formal Wildlife Board recommendation on the record, rather than an informal staff answer. If granted it legalizes the species statewide; if denied, the applicant may request agency action before the Wildlife Board within 30 days (R657-2).

targets.name: Utah Office of Administrative Rules — Petition for Rulemaking (Utah Code 63G-3-601) / Public Notice Website
targets.why: Any person may petition a state agency to amend an existing rule under Utah Code 63G-3-601 (Office of Administrative Rules, rules.utah.gov, phone 801-957-7110). If DWR opens any rulemaking touching R657-3b or Table 3b-1, the proposed-rule notice, comment-period dates (typically 30+ days), and agency contact are posted on the Utah Public Notice Website (utah.gov/pmn) and in the twice-monthly Utah State Bulletin — the place a well-supported species-addition comment lands on the formal record. No roof-rat-specific window is open now; watch this portal.

template.en:
To: Utah Division of Wildlife Resources — Wildlife Registration / Certificate of Registration Office
Re: Classification of captive-bred domestic roof rat (Rattus rattus) under Rule R657-3b / Bird and Mammal Classification Table 3b-1

Dear Wildlife Registration Office,

I am writing about a gap in Bird and Mammal Classification Table 3b-1. The table names the Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus) — the species behind the common pet 'fancy rat' — as a domestic animal not covered by R657-3b, but the closely related roof rat (Rattus rattus) is not listed at all, which leaves it 'presumed prohibited' by default and assessable only through a Certificate of Registration.

This appears to be a recent and possibly inadvertent change. Until the May 1, 2023 rule rewrite, the prior rule R657-3(32) jointly exempted 'Rats, Norway and Black (Rattus norvegicus and Rattus rattus)' as non-COR domestic pets. The 2023 simplification carried over only the Norway rat, dropping the roof rat — with no published finding that domesticated roof rats are dangerous.

The animals at issue are captive-bred, selectively bred for tameness, kept strictly indoors as pets, and never released to the wild. They are domesticated companion rodents, no different in keeping from the Norway-rat fancy rat the table already exempts. The distinction is species enumeration, not domestication or any public-safety concern.

I respectfully ask the Division to: (1) tell me in writing whether the post-2023 omission of R. rattus from Table 3b-1 was intentional, and whether captive-bred R. rattus is treated as unlisted-and-assessable or can be grouped with R. norvegicus as a domestic strain; and (2) advise what a Request for Species Reclassification under R657-3a-8 to restore captive-bred Rattus rattus to Table 3b-1's noncontrolled/domestic-exempt section would require. Thank you for your time and for considering this correction.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your city, Utah] / [Your email]

kit.confidence_notes: Verified 2026-06-10 via Gemini Deep Research against official Utah sources. CONFIRMED: (1) Table 3b-1 (May 1, 2023) lists 'Rat, Norway (Rattus norvegicus)' under 'Domestic mammals and mammalian livestock not covered under this rule' and entirely omits Rattus rattus; R657-3b's default makes unlisted species 'presumed prohibited... require an assessment before collection, importation or possession will be authorized.' (2) Lawful pathways exist and are itemized: COR before collecting/possessing prohibited-or-controlled species (R657-3b-8), before propagating (R657-3b-13), before transporting (R657-3b-11) and importing (R657-3b-10); plus R657-3a-8 Species Reclassification and R657-3a-9 Variance, each $200, with COR issuance fees ($10 handling + $75 personal / $150 commercial, $30 renewal) and a 30-day Wildlife Board appeal under R657-2. (3) The pre-2023 joint exemption is documented: old R657-3(32) listed 'Rats, Norway and Black (Rattus norvegicus and Rattus rattus)' (Utah State Bulletin 2012/2015), severed in the May 2023 R657-3 -> R657-3a/3b/3c rewrite per the RAC/AAG memo. (4) Import dual-agency layer confirmed: UDAF R58-1-13 bars importing species prohibited under R657-3 and requires a CVI + entry permit for any animal needing a DWR COR. (5) COR-office contact verified: dwrregistration@utah.gov / anitacandelaria@utah.gov, 801-538-4701, 1594 W. North Temple Box 146301 SLC UT 84114-6301; transfer barred by Utah Code 23A-5-309. OPEN per DR: whether the omission was deliberate biosecurity policy or clerical (Norway-rat-as-catch-all); whether pre-2023 animals are grandfathered; the evidentiary burden for reclassification (high, given pest-manual classification). This is a research aid, not legal advice; confirm classification directly with DWR before acquiring animals.

keep.why: Bird and Mammal Classification Table 3b-1 (incorporated by Utah Admin. Code R657-3b) lists 'Rat, Norway / Rattus norvegicus' as a domestic animal not covered by the rule, but does NOT list Rattus rattus. The table's header makes every unlisted species 'presumed prohibited... require an assessment before... possession will be authorized,' and R657-3b-8 requires a Certificate of Registration before collecting/possessing any prohibited or controlled species. So possessing a captive-bred roof rat is not automatically illegal — a lawful COR pathway exists via a species assessment / variance — but it cannot proceed without prior DWR authorization, and unauthorized possession is a violation of Utah Code 23A-5-309. Restricted, not prohibited.
keep.governing_law: Utah Admin. Code R657-3b-8 + Bird and Mammal Classification Table 3b-1 (May 1, 2023); pathways R657-3a-8 (reclassification) / R657-3a-9 (variance); Utah Code 23A-5-309.

breed.why: R657-3b-13 requires a Certificate of Registration before propagating any species classified as prohibited or controlled. Because R. rattus is unlisted on Table 3b-1 (presumed prohibited pending assessment), breeding can't proceed without a favorable DWR assessment and a COR that affirmatively authorizes propagation — which 'may contain stipulations to prevent detrimental impacts to wild populations, the environment, or human health or safety.' No exemption applies (the table names R. norvegicus, not R. rattus). A lawful pathway exists, so this is restricted; the DR notes the propagation burden is higher than mere possession given the species' pest-manual classification.
breed.governing_law: Utah Admin. Code R657-3b-13; Bird and Mammal Classification Table 3b-1 (default = presumed prohibited); pathway R657-3a-9 (variance) / R657-3a-8 (reclassification).

sell_give.why: Utah Code 23A-5-309 bars collecting, possessing, transporting, donating, transferring, or exporting protected wildlife except as authorized by a rule, proclamation, or Wildlife Board order. Because R. rattus is unlisted / presumed prohibited, any sale or gift is lawful only to a recipient who already holds the necessary DWR COR for the species — transferring to an unregistered Utah resident implicates both parties. A commercial storefront additionally needs local municipal pet-shop/dealer licensing and zoning approval, which the COR application requires be resolved first. A pathway exists (transfer between COR holders), so restricted, not prohibited.
sell_give.governing_law: Utah Code 23A-5-309; Utah Admin. Code R657-3b + Table 3b-1; local municipal pet-shop/dealer ordinances.

transport.why: Intrastate movement of an unlisted/presumed-prohibited mammal triggers a COR (R657-3b-11); even moving a legally held roof rat between Utah counties must be covered by the COR. Importation compounds the requirement: a COR is required before importing (R657-3b-10), and UDAF Rule R58-1-13 makes it unlawful to import any species prohibited under R657-3, requiring a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) plus a UDAF entry permit for any animal that needs a DWR COR. A lawful path exists (COR + CVI + entry permit), so restricted. Never release a roof rat.
transport.governing_law: Utah Admin. Code R657-3b-10 / R657-3b-11; UDAF Rule R58-1-13; Bird and Mammal Classification Table 3b-1.

restrictions.summary: Because R. rattus is unlisted on Table 3b-1 (only the Norway rat is domestic-exempt), it is 'presumed prohibited' and requires a DWR Certificate of Registration before possession, breeding, sale, or import. The COR is reached either through a case-by-case Request for Variance (R657-3a-9) or a statewide Request for Species Reclassification (R657-3a-8). Both require an interagency review (DWR + Dept. of Agriculture & Food + Dept. of Health & Human Services). Contact the DWR Wildlife Registration office BEFORE acquiring any animals.
steps: Contact the DWR Wildlife Registration / COR office (dwrregistration@utah.gov) about classification and a species assessment for captive-bred R. rattus

File a Request for Variance (R657-3a-9) for personal possession/breeding, OR a Request for Species Reclassification (R657-3a-8) to restore R. rattus to the noncontrolled/domestic-exempt list ($200 each)
If a variance/assessment is granted, apply for the COR ($10 handling + $75 personal or $150 commercial; $30 renewal) and meet caging/husbandry/inspection stipulations
Resolve local municipal/county zoning and pet-shop/dealer licensing first (required before the COR application)
For import: obtain a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection and a UDAF entry permit (R58-1-13)
If denied: request agency action before the Wildlife Board within 30 days (R657-2)

restrictions.where_to_file: Utah Division of Wildlife Resources — Wildlife Registration / COR office, 1594 W. North Temple, Suite 2110, Box 146301, Salt Lake City, UT 84114-6301 (import permit: Utah Dept of Agriculture & Food, Animal Industry)
restrictions.fees: Species reclassification or variance request $200 each; COR $10 handling + $75 personal / $150 commercial issuance, $30 renewal, $10 amendment; UDAF CVI + entry permit fees for import.

restrictions.summary: Never release or abandon a roof rat in Utah. The state classifies Rattus rattus in its Vertebrate Pest and Structural Pest manuals as a highly destructive non-native invasive pest and a zoonotic-disease vector; release of a held animal would compound the criminal exposure under Utah Code 23A-5-309 and the ecological concerns that drive the COR review. Rehome only to a lawfully authorized (COR-holding) recipient.
steps: Keep roof rats strictly indoors; never release
Rehome only to a COR-authorized recipient

inquiry_focus: Table 3b-1 (May 1, 2023) lists 'Rat, Norway (Rattus norvegicus)' as a domestic animal not covered by R657-3b but omits Rattus rattus, leaving it 'presumed prohibited, requires assessment' — even though pre-2023 rule R657-3(32) jointly exempted both rat species. (1) Was the 2023 omission of R. rattus intentional biosecurity policy or a clerical assumption that 'Norway rat' covered all pet rats? (2) Are pre-2023 captive-bred roof rats grandfathered, or do their owners now need a COR? (3) Would DWR group captive-bred, domestic-lineage R. rattus with R. norvegicus, or require an R657-3a-9 variance / R657-3a-8 reclassification? (4) What evidentiary threshold would the interagency panel (DWR + UDAF + DHHS) require to restore captive-bred R. rattus to the noncontrolled/domestic-exempt list?
